sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish objective information from subjective information in patient documentation.
- Document observable facts rather than personal interpretations or opinions.
- Apply documentation standards for accuracy, timeliness, and completeness.
- Quote patients accurately and record subjective data in the patient's own words.
- Use neutral, person-centered language that is free of judgment and stigma.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Objective means anyone would see or measure the same thing, like reading the number on a thermometer. It is not just one person's thought or feeling.

### Question 2

Subjective is what only the patient knows, like whether their tummy hurts. No one else can measure that from the outside.

### Question 3

Just because someone says something out loud does not make it a fact you can measure. 'My stomach hurts' is still only what that person feels.

### Question 4

A thermometer shows a number that anyone can read. That number is a fact, which makes it objective.

### Question 5

Blood pressure is like the gas gauge in a car; it shows a number anyone can read, not a guess.

### Question 6

Dizziness is like feeling sleepy; no one else can see it, so it is only what the patient tells us.

### Question 7

The scale shows a number everyone can see, so weight is objective, just like measuring flour for a recipe.

### Question 8

Counting a pulse is like counting pennies; it is a number you get by measuring, not by guessing.

### Question 9

A pain score is still the patient's own feeling, just put into a number so we can compare it over time.

### Question 10

Only the patient knows whether they slept, so their story is subjective, like telling someone about a dream.

### Question 11

Objective things can be measured with tools, like a thermometer or scale, while feelings are things only the patient can tell us.

### Question 12

If the patient has to tell us about it from inside their body, it is subjective; if we can measure or see it, it is objective.

### Question 13

Vital signs are numbers we get from tools, like a thermometer, so they are objective facts.

### Question 14

Even if a family member says it, a symptom is still a story someone is telling, not a number we measured.

### Question 15

If you can see it happen with your own eyes, like someone limping, that is objective, just like seeing rain through a window.

### Question 16

Objective facts are like a shared ruler; everyone gets the same measurement, so we can trust them more.

### Question 17

A machine cannot tell us how much something hurts; only the patient can, so we write down what they say.

### Question 18

A fact is like 'the sky is blue'; an interpretation is like 'it will rain later.' One you see, the other you guess.

### Question 19

Accurate means writing down exactly what happened, like copying a phone number digit by digit without guessing any numbers.

### Question 20

It is like writing down a homework assignment as soon as the teacher gives it, so you do not forget it by the end of class.

### Question 21

A complete note is like packing everything you need for a trip; missing one important item can cause problems later.

### Question 22

Quoting is like repeating a friend's joke word for word so you do not accidentally change the punchline.

### Question 23

Judgmental words are like calling someone 'lazy' instead of saying they sat down; one is a label, the other is what you saw.

### Question 24

It is like saying 'she said she is tired' instead of 'she is being dramatic'; one repeats the words, the other adds a mean label.

### Question 25

A time stamp is like the timestamp on a text message; it tells everyone when it actually happened.

### Question 26

The numbers from the machines are facts, but 'my head is throbbing' is a feeling only the patient can report.

### Question 27

Write what the person actually said in quotes, like copying their words, instead of deciding how they feel for them.

### Question 28

Instead of calling someone 'bad at following rules,' just say exactly what they told you, like 'I missed two doses.'

### Question 29

Say what you saw, like 'they stumbled and smelled like alcohol,' instead of deciding 'they are drunk,' because you only know the clues.

### Question 30

Never guess a number in a chart; it is like making up a test score. Go measure again or ask someone who knows.

### Question 31

Say what happened, like 'they raised their voice and said these exact words,' instead of calling them 'angry.'

### Question 32

Just say what time they arrived, like '20 minutes late,' instead of guessing they did not care.

### Question 33

The assistant's job is to pass the paper to the teacher, not to grade it; the provider decides what the result means.

### Question 34

Fix a mistake with one clean line through it and your initials, like crossing out a wrong answer but still being able to see it.

### Question 35

Read it back like repeating a phone number out loud so the person can say 'yes, that is right.'

### Question 36

A name and birthday are like a unique key that opens only the right locker; if they are wrong, you open the wrong one.

### Question 37

Be like a stopwatch and say the exact time, not 'around morning,' so everyone knows exactly when it happened.

### Question 38

If the recipe on a food label is wrong, someone could get sick; a wrong medicine list works the same way.

### Question 39

If a store writes your address wrong, you can ask them to fix it; HIPAA gives patients a similar way to ask for corrections.

### Question 40

If your handwriting looks like scribbles, someone might read '15' as '75,' just like a sloppy note at school.

### Question 41

If you turn in homework late, you label it late instead of pretending you did it on time; notes work the same way.

### Question 42

It is easier to remember what you had for breakfast right now than a week later; writing it down right away keeps it accurate.

### Question 43

If there is no receipt, it is hard to prove you bought something; a chart entry is the 'receipt' that care happened.

### Question 44

If a question on a form was not answered, write 'not provided' instead of making up an answer or leaving a confusing gap.

### Question 45

Sometimes saying 'the patient does NOT have a fever' is just as important as saying they do; it is a clue the doctor needs.

### Question 46

If someone says 'I feel a little off' and you write 'I feel terrible,' you changed their meaning; always use their words.

### Question 47

Paraphrasing is like summarizing a story for a friend; keep the important parts and the same meaning, and do not add your own twist.

### Question 48

Write what the patient asked and why they said they need it, instead of calling them a name like 'drug-seeker.'

### Question 49

Say 'a kid with glasses,' not 'a glasses kid'; the person comes first, and the condition is just one part of them.

### Question 50

Describe exactly what happened, like a camera recording it, instead of giving it a name like 'a tantrum.'

### Question 51

If your sister tells you something about your friend, you say 'my sister said...' so everyone knows who said it.

### Question 52

Their own words are the most truthful record of what they feel, like taking a voice memo instead of retelling it from memory.

### Question 53

Describing what you see, like 'red and swollen,' is objective, just like describing a picture without saying what it means.

### Question 54

Put the measured number and the patient's own words together, like 'the scale says 150' plus 'they said they feel heavy.'

### Question 55

Writing 'I doubt it' is like a referee picking a side; a good record only reports what happened, not who the writer believes.

### Question 56

A good record is like a shared notebook everyone can read, so the next helper knows exactly what happened before.

### Question 57

Anything that names a patient and talks about their health is private, like a secret that must be locked up and shared only with the right people.

### Question 58

Only take as much as you need for the job, like grabbing one file instead of carrying the whole cabinet.

### Question 59

If a customer says the receipt is wrong, you follow the store's return process; the assistant follows the office's correction process.

### Question 60

Data integrity means the information stays truthful and unbroken, like a lock that shows if someone has opened the box.

### Question 61

A fact plus a guess, like 'he coughed (fact) and he is faking (guess),' means you should keep the fact and drop the guess.

### Question 62

'My head hurts' is the patient's feeling, but 'they are rubbing their head' is something you saw, so one is subjective and one is objective.

### Question 63

Keep the 'what I measured' and 'what they told me' in separate baskets so no one mixes up a fact with a feeling.

### Question 64

Do not try to write while juggling; finish the task and double-check it, like proofreading homework before turning it in.

### Question 65

Check the spelling in the book before writing it down, like looking up a word you are not sure how to spell.

### Question 66

Write down the exact feeling they described, like 'a burning sensation,' instead of deciding what disease it is.

### Question 67

A chart is like a witness in a notebook; it must tell the truth because people may rely on it later.

### Question 68

Saying someone 'looks sad' is a guess; saying 'they cried and said they feel sad' is what you actually saw and heard.

### Question 69

Write their exact words, like 'eating whatever I want,' instead of calling them names for it.

### Question 70

If someone says their chest hurts, write down their words and tell the grown-up in charge right away, like reporting an emergency.

### Question 71

A notebook written at the time is better than anyone's memory later, like checking a receipt when there is a disagreement at the store.

### Question 72

A pain number is still the patient's own feeling, but putting it on a 0-to-10 ladder helps us see if it goes up or down over time.

### Question 73

Do not sign your name on work you did not do, just like you would not sign someone else's test paper.

### Question 74

Listen, write it down, and repeat it back, like echoing a phone number so the other person can catch any mistake.

### Question 75

Instead of 'uncooperative,' say what they did, like 'would not sit on the exam table,' so readers know the actual behavior.

### Question 76

Knowing whether the story came from the patient or their sister matters, just like knowing who told you a rumor.

### Question 77

If you do not understand a word, ask what it means before writing it down, like asking a teacher to explain a new word.

### Question 78

Say what happened and what they said, like 'they said no today and want to think,' instead of calling them names.

### Question 79

Jot down the important facts right away, like taking quick notes in class so you do not forget them by the weekend.

### Question 80

When unsure, write down what you know is true and ask the supervisor about the rest, like raising your hand in class.

### Question 81

'Doing well' is like saying a cake 'turned out good'; tell people what you actually saw so they know why.

### Question 82

Safety comes from writing down the true numbers and telling the right person when something seems wrong.

### Question 83

Keep the important parts and the patient's own words, like writing a book report with the key events and quotes.

### Question 84

Sort them from the mean label 'lazy' down to the true words 'I feel too tired to walk,' like ranking guesses from least to most true.

### Question 85

Read over your work to catch mistakes, like checking your math before turning in a test.
